L9@P0: Autotomy, the voluntary shedding of
L10@P0: a body part, is common to distantlyrelated animals such as arthropods,
L11@P0: gastropods, asteroids, amphibians, and
L12@P0: lizards1,2. Autotomy is generally followed
L13@P0: by regeneration of shed terminal body
L14@P0: parts, such as appendages or tails.
L15@P0: Here, we identify a new type of extreme
L16@P0: autotomy in two species of sacoglossan
L17@P0: sea slug (Mollusca: Gastropoda).
L18@P0: Surprisingly, they shed the main
L19@P0: body, including the whole heart, and
L20@P0: regenerated a new body. In contrast, the
L21@P0: Correspondence shed body did not regenerate the head.
L22@P0: These sacoglossans can incorporate
L23@P0: chloroplasts from algal food into their
L24@P0: cells to utilise for photosynthesis
L25@P0: (kleptoplasty3), and we propose that
L26@P0: this unique characteristic may facilitate
L27@P0: survival after autotomy and subsequent
L28@P0: regeneration.

L101@P1: In contrast, none of 64 parasite-free

L104@P1: These two sacoglossan ‘species’
L105@P1: have a transverse groove at their neck,
L106@P1: which appears to be a predetermined
L107@P1: ‘breakage plane’ (Figure 1I). We gently
L108@P1: tied this part using a fi ne nylon string
L109@P1: in six individuals of Elysia cf. marginata
L110@P1: (Methods S1A–E). Five of them
L111@P1: autotomised at the tied position within a
L112@P1: day (Methods S1E). The tied position of
L113@P1: the remaining individual shifted slightly
L114@P1: lower, and it autotomised at the neck 9
L115@P1: days after treatment. Their autotomised
L116@P1: bodies represented 80–85% of the total
L117@P1: weight. In contrast, imitated predator
L118@P1: attacks, like pinching of the head
L119@P1: and cutting of the parapodia (lateral
L120@P1: extensions), did not induce autotomy
L121@P1: (see Supplemental Experimental
L122@P1: Procedures).
L123@P1: Both Elysia cf. marginata and
L124@P1: E. atroviridis shed the main body,
L125@P1: including the heart. Some other
L126@P1: sea slugs also autotomise, but they
L127@P1: shed minor body parts such as
L128@P1: tails, parapodia, or dorsal papillae1
L129@P1: .
L130@P1: Other invertebrates (e.g., cnidarians,
L131@P1: planarians, and asteroids) can regenerate
L132@P1: their main body following division. Also,
L133@P1: some amphibians are known to have
L134@P1: a high regeneration capacity, including
L135@P1: tails, limbs, eyes, and even the heart
L136@P1: ventricle5. However, autotomy in this
L137@P1: study is remarkable in that animals with
L138@P1: complex body plans can survive even if
L139@P1: they lose the main body, including the
L140@P1: heart, and subsequently regenerate the
L141@P1: whole lost area.The reason why the
L142@P1: head can survive without the heart and
L143@P1: other important organs is unclear. We
L144@P1: have succeeded in a complete rearing
L145@P1: of Elysia cf. marginata for multiple
L146@P1: generations — thus, they can be used as
L147@P1: a model system for studying autotomy
L148@P1: and regeneration of the body.
L149@P1: The function of this large-scale
L150@P1: autotomy remains unclear at present.
L151@P1: Most animals, including some
L152@P1: sacoglossans1,2, are considered to
L153@P1: autotomise to escape predation.
L154@P1: However, adult sacoglossans generally
L155@P1: have few predators due to their cryptic
L156@P1: coloration and presence of toxic
L157@P1: chemicals incorporated from their food3,6
L158@P1: (but see Nakano et al.7). Our experiments
L159@P1: also showed that autotomy of E. cf.
L160@P1: marginata took several hours, which is
L161@P1: not effective to avoid predation, and that
L162@P1: imitated predator attacks did not induce
L163@P1: autotomy. Therefore, their autotomy
L164@P1: is unlikely to function as predation
L165@P1: escape. We suggest that removing
L166@P1: internal parasites is a likely function of
L167@P1: autotomy, at least in E. atroviridis. All
L168@P1: autotomised individuals (and autolysed
L169@P1: ones as well) had a parasite, and after
L170@P1: regeneration they became parasitefree. The parasites occupy most of the
L171@P1: main body of E. atroviridis and strongly
L172@P1: inhibit its reproduction during lifetime
L173@P1: ( data not shown). Thus, removing such
L174@P1: parasites by autotomy likely enhances
L175@P1: the host’s reproductive success. Elysia
L176@P1: cf. marginata did not appear to have
L177@P1: parasites in our culture, but this species
L178@P1: complex has another congeneric
L179@P1: parasite8
L180@P1: . Such ‘parasitic autotomy’ has
L181@P1: been shown in earthworms to counteract
L182@P1: a protozoan parasite9. Alternatively,
L183@P1: but not mutually exclusive to this idea,
L184@P1: autotomy by the sacoglossans may
L185@P1: function to escape from being tangled
L186@P1: in algae or to remove accumulated toxic
L187@P1: chemicals.
L188@P1: The body shedding of the
L189@P1: sacoglossans appears to, fi rstly, have
L190@P1: a defensive function (to eliminate
L191@P1: endoparasites); secondly, occur by an
L192@P1: intrinsic mechanism; and thirdly, be a
L193@P1: controlled loss. All of these are conditions
L194@P1: often used to distinguish autotomy from
L195@P1: other losses of body parts1
L196@P1: . Why these
L197@P1: sacoglossans can regenerate their body
L198@P1: even if they lose most organs remains
L199@P1: unclear, but we suspect involvement of
L200@P1: kleptoplasty. In Elysia, a highly branched
L201@P1: digestive gland is spread over the
L202@P1: majority of its body surface, including the
L203@P1: head, and the gland is lined by cells that
L204@P1: maintain ingested algal chloroplasts4
L205@P1: .
L206@P1: Thus, these sacoglossans can obtain
L207@P1: energy for survival and regeneration from
L208@P1: photosynthesis by kleptoplasts, even
L209@P1: when they cannot digest food10. Further
L210@P1: investigation of autotomy in these and
L211@P1: other sacoglossans will elucidate its
L212@P1: function, mechanism, and evolutionary
L213@P1: origin.
